sections.b: Numbers opens with a count. Moses and Aaron enroll "every male twenty years old and up who could go out to war," tribe by tribe (1:2–3), and the total is 603,550 (1:46), the same figure as the silver count of Exodus 38:26. The Levites are left out of the army roll (1:47–49) and counted on their own from one month old: 22,000 (3:39). Each tribal total is a round number to the hundred, except Gad's 45,650. Readers take the figures in four main ways. Many traditional Jewish and Christian readers take them as plain head counts. Flinders Petrie and later George Mendenhall and Colin Humphreys read 'elef as a unit or clan, not a thousand, which gives an army of some thousands. Others look for symbolic or number-value patterns. Critical scholars such as Martin Noth see the lists as later priestly work that projects a large nation back into the desert.

common: The census shows God keeping his promise to Abraham that his family would grow into a great people.
uncommon: Petrie read the totals as 'clans' and 'hundreds,' giving only about 5,550 fighting men in the first count.

sections.b: Numbers 5:11–31 sets out what happens when a husband is seized by "a spirit of jealousy" and has no witness against his wife (5:13–14). He brings her to the priest with a grain offering of jealousy. The priest loosens her hair, puts her under oath and makes her drink holy water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor and the washed-off ink of the curses (5:17–24). If she is guilty, "her belly will swell and her thigh will waste away"; if she is innocent, "she will not be harmed, and she will be able to have children" (5:27–28). Read honestly, the rite applies only to wives, and the husband is "free from guilt" whatever happens (5:31). Defenders point out that it takes the case out of the husband's hands and away from mob violence, and that the drink itself is harmless unless God acts. Tikva Frymer-Kensky studied it as a legal ordeal, and Alice Bach as a text about male fear. The Mishnah says Yohanan ben Zakkai stopped the rite when adultery became common (Mishnah Sotah 9:9).

common: The ritual let God himself judge a case that no human court could prove.
uncommon: Some read 'her thigh will fall away' as a miscarriage, so that the rite worked as an abortion of a child conceived in adultery.

sections.b: God gives Aaron's sons fixed words to bless Israel: "May the LORD bless you and keep you. May the LORD make his face shine toward you and be gracious to you. May the LORD lift up his face toward you and grant you peace" (6:24–26). The three lines grow from three to five to seven Hebrew words, and the divine name stands in each line. The point is stated next: "So they will put my name on the Israelites, and I myself will bless them" (6:27). The priests speak, but God blesses. Two small silver scrolls found at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem in 1979 carry a shorter form of the blessing. Gabriel Barkay dated them to about 600 BC, before the Babylonian exile. A few scholars argue for a later, Hellenistic date, but new imaging in 2004 supported the earlier one. Synagogues still use the blessing in the priests' raised-hands rite, and many churches end their services with it.

common: The blessing's three-part shape and the threefold divine name have long been read by Christians as a hint of the Trinity.
uncommon: Some scholars think the Ketef Hinnom amulets show the blessing in an older, shorter form, and that Numbers 6 expanded it.

sections.b: Numbers is called Bemidbar, "In the wilderness," after its first verse. Chapters 1–10 show the wilderness at its most orderly. The tribes camp in a square around the tent of meeting, three to each side (2:1–34), and the Levites form an inner ring (3:23–38). The cloud decides when they move: "At the LORD's word they camped, and at the LORD's word they set out" (9:23). Silver trumpets sound the march (10:1–10), and the ark goes ahead "to scout out a resting place for them" (10:33). Then, in chapter 11, the complaining begins. Many readers see this contrast as the book's design: Israel is ready to go, and the first generation still fails.

common: The wilderness was a school where God taught Israel to depend on him day by day.
uncommon: Some critical scholars read the ordered camp of Numbers 2 as an idealized picture of the later temple and its city, not a memory of desert life.

sections.b: Numbers 6:1–21 lets a man or a woman make "an extraordinary vow, a Nazirite vow, to be set apart for the LORD" (6:2). For the time of the vow the Nazirite keeps three rules. He drinks no wine and eats nothing from the grapevine. No razor touches his head. He goes near no dead body, not even a parent's (6:3–7). If someone dies suddenly beside him, he must shave and start over (6:9–12). At the end he brings offerings and burns his hair in the fire under the peace offering (6:18). The vow was meant to be for a set time, though Samson and Samuel were set apart for life (Judges 13:5; 1 Samuel 1:11). Paul seems to have kept a similar vow (Acts 18:18; Acts 21:23–26). The rabbis argued over whether the Nazirite is holy or a sinner who needs a sin offering for denying himself wine (Bavli Nazir 19a).
sections.refs: Numbers 6:1–21; Judges 13:5; 1 Samuel 1:11; Amos 2:11–12; Acts 18:18; Acts 21:23–26

common: The Nazirite gave ordinary Israelites a way to live for a time with a holiness like the high priest's.
uncommon: Some think John the Baptist, who drank no wine (Luke 1:15), was a lifelong Nazirite.

sections.h: The tribes in camp and on the march
sections.b: Numbers 1–10 lists the twelve tribes again and again: in the census (1:5–43), around the tent (2:1–31), as twelve leaders bringing gifts on twelve days (7:12–83) and in the order of march (10:14–28). Levi is taken out of the twelve and given to the tent, and Joseph is split into Ephraim and Manasseh, so the count stays at twelve. Judah camps on the east and marches first (2:3; 10:14), which many readers link with Jacob's words about Judah's scepter. Reuben, the firstborn, comes second. The repetition shows every tribe with an equal share in the worship and the army.

common: The equal gifts of chapter 7 show that each tribe had the same standing before God.
uncommon: Some critical scholars think the different tribal orders in Numbers reflect lists from different periods.

sections.b: Numbers 3–4 and 8 draw a sharp line between Aaron's sons and the rest of Levi. Only the priests may cover the holy things; the Kohathites carry them but "must not touch the holy things. If they do, they will die" (4:15). The Levites are "given" to Aaron (3:9; 8:19) and keep guard around the tent, so that no plague strikes the people when they come near (8:19). They work from age thirty (4:3) or twenty-five (8:24) to fifty. Many critical scholars, following Julius Wellhausen, think this two-level clergy reflects the time after the exile (compare Ezekiel 44:10–16). Jacob Milgrom argued that the guard duty is old and fits other ancient temples.

common: The Levites protect Israel by standing between the people and the holy place.
uncommon: Some trace the Levites' lower rank to the country priests whom Josiah brought to Jerusalem but kept from the altar (2 Kings 23:8–9).

sections.h: Levites in place of the firstborn
sections.b: In Egypt God claimed Israel's firstborn: "On the day I struck down all the firstborn of Egypt, I made every firstborn in Israel holy to me" (3:13). Numbers 3 swaps the Levites for them: "The Levites belong to me" (3:12). Moses counts 22,273 firstborn males against 22,000 Levites, and the extra 273 are bought back at five shekels each (3:43–51). Readers have long noted that 22,273 firstborn is very few for 603,550 men, which is one reason some doubt the large census figures. Rashi and others explain the swap as the firstborn losing the role at the golden calf, when Levi stood with Moses.

common: The Levites stand in for the firstborn whom God spared at the Passover.
uncommon: Some think the low count of firstborn means only those born after the exodus were counted.

sections.h: Setting up and carrying the tent
sections.b: Numbers 7:1 begins on the day "Moses finished putting up the tabernacle," the day of Exodus 40. From here the tent is a building that moves. Chapter 4 says who wraps and who carries each part: the Kohathites carry the ark, table, lampstand and altars, the Gershonites the curtains, and the Merarites the frames, posts and bases. The tribal leaders give six covered carts and twelve oxen, but the Kohathites get none, since they carry the holy things on their shoulders (7:6–9). David's first attempt to move the ark on a cart ended in Uzzah's death (2 Samuel 6:3–7).

common: The tabernacle at the center of the camp shows God living among his people.
uncommon: Some scholars think the portable tent of Numbers is a model of the later temple imagined back into the desert.

sections.b: Numbers 5:1–4 orders three kinds of people sent out of the camp: "everyone with a skin disease, everyone who has a discharge, and everyone who is unclean because of a dead body" (5:2). They are sent out for the sake of the camp itself, "so that they do not make their camps unclean, the camps where I live among them" (5:3). The same concern drives the second Passover. Men unclean from a dead body cannot keep the feast on the set day, so God allows a make-up date a month later (9:6–12). The ashes of the red heifer for cleansing come later, in Numbers 19.

common: Uncleanness is not sin, but it cannot be brought near the holy God.
uncommon: Some readers see the rules as early public health, though most scholars see them as about holiness rather than germs.

sections.b: Numbers 9 records the first Passover kept after Egypt, at Sinai in the first month of the second year (9:1–5). Some men were unclean from a dead body and asked, "Why should we be shut out from presenting the LORD's offering at its set time?" (9:7). God gives a second date, the fourteenth of the second month, for the unclean and for those on a far journey (9:10–11). But one who could keep it and does not "is to be cut off from his people" (9:13). The foreigner may keep it under "one rule" (9:14). Hezekiah later used the second-month date (2 Chronicles 30:2–3), and Jewish tradition still marks Pesach Sheni.

common: The second Passover shows God making room for those kept back through no fault of their own.
uncommon: Some critical scholars think the second-month date grew out of Hezekiah's late Passover rather than the other way around.

sections.b: Numbers 9:15–23 describes the cloud over the tabernacle: by day it covered the tent, "and at night it looked like fire" (9:16). When it lifted, Israel set out; when it settled, they camped, whether "two days, a month or a longer time" (9:22). The passage repeats "at the LORD's word" seven times. In 7:89 Moses hears "the voice speaking to him from above the atonement lid," so the glory both leads the march and speaks in the tent.

common: The cloud shows God guiding his people step by step.
uncommon: Some suggest the cloud and fire picture a column of incense or signal fire carried before the camp.

sections.b: Numbers 10:33 says that on the three days' journey from the mountain, "the ark of the LORD's covenant went in front of them, to scout out a resting place for them." When it set out, Moses said, "Rise up, LORD! Let your enemies scatter"; when it rested, "Return, LORD, to the tens of thousands of Israel's clans" (10:35–36). Psalm 68 opens with the same cry. In Hebrew manuscripts these two verses are set off by inverted letter nuns, and the Talmud calls them a book of their own (Bavli Shabbat 115b–116a). The Greek translation puts verse 34 after them.

common: The ark going first shows God himself leading Israel into the land.
uncommon: Some rabbis held that the two verses were moved here from another place in Numbers.

sections.h: The lamps lit toward the front
sections.b: Numbers 8:1–4 tells Aaron to set up the seven lamps so that they "shine forward, toward the front of the lampstand" (8:2). The lampstand is hammered from gold and "to match the vision the LORD had shown him" (8:4). Coming right after the leaders' gifts of chapter 7, the passage moved Rashi to say that Aaron was told his share in the dedication was greater, since he would light the lamps.

common: The lamps shining forward picture God's light given to his people.
uncommon: Carol Meyers traced the lampstand's shape to ancient tree and plant designs.

sections.b: Before Israel leaves Sinai, Moses asks "Hobab son of Reuel the Midianite, Moses' father-in-law" to come along (10:29). Hobab says no at first, and Moses presses him: "You know this wilderness and where to pitch our tents. You can be our eyes" (10:31). The verse's grammar makes it unclear whether Hobab or Reuel is the father-in-law, and Judges 4:11 calls Hobab Moses' father-in-law. The text never says whether Hobab went, though Judges 1:16 places his Kenite descendants in Judah. Some readers see a tension with the cloud guiding Israel; others see human guides and God's guidance working together.

common: Hobab is often taken to be Jethro's son and so Moses' brother-in-law.
uncommon: Some think Jethro, Reuel and Hobab are names from different traditions for the same man.

sections.b: The list of Aaron's sons in Numbers 3 stops to recall the deaths: "Nadab and Abihu died before the LORD in the wilderness of Sinai, when they brought strange fire near before the LORD. They had no sons" (3:4). So the priesthood passes through Eleazar and Ithamar. The note is short, but it stands at the head of the Levite rules, where touching holy things wrongly means death (4:15, 20).

common: Their deaths warn that God must be approached in the way he commands.
uncommon: Some rabbis said they died for teaching law in front of Moses, their teacher.

sections.b: Numbers 7 is the longest chapter in the Torah. Each of the twelve leaders brings the same gift on his own day: a silver plate and bowl full of flour, a gold pan of incense, animals for burnt, sin and peace offerings (7:12–83). The text repeats every list in full rather than saying "the same." Rabbinic readers took this to mean that each tribe's gift was precious in its own right; Numbers Rabbah even gives each leader a different meaning for the same items. The totals come at the end: twelve plates, twelve bowls and twelve pans (7:84–88).

common: The repetition honors each tribe's gift equally.
uncommon: Some scholars think the chapter was copied from a temple archive of gifts.

sections.b: After the priestly blessing God says, "So they will put my name on the Israelites, and I myself will bless them" (6:27). The name is the LORD (YHWH), spoken three times in the blessing. In the Second Temple the priests said the name aloud in this blessing, while outside the temple a substitute was used (Mishnah Sotah 7:6). The Ketef Hinnom scrolls are among the oldest objects to carry a biblical text with the name YHWH; older inscriptions with the name, such as the Mesha Stele and the Kuntillet Ajrud jars, do not quote Scripture.

common: To bear God's name is to belong to him.
uncommon: Some read 'put my name' as a physical act, like wearing an amulet such as those from Ketef Hinnom.

sections.b: Numbers 10:1–10 tells Moses to make two trumpets of hammered silver. These are chatsotsrot, long straight metal trumpets, not the curved ram's horn, the shofar. The priests blow them, and the signals are coded. A long blast (taqa') on both gathers the whole community, on one only the leaders. A loud, broken "battle blast" (teru'ah) sets the camps on the march (10:3–7). In war they sound the alarm, "Then the LORD your God will remember you" (10:9). At feasts and new moons they sound over the offerings (10:10). Josephus describes the trumpet as a little under a cubit long, narrow, with a bell at the end (Antiquities 3.291). Two trumpets from the tomb of Tutankhamun, one silver and one bronze, show what such instruments looked like, and the Arch of Titus in Rome shows trumpets carried off from the temple in AD 70. Priests blow them in war at 31:6 and in 2 Chronicles 13:12–14, and at the temple's dedication (2 Chronicles 5:12–13). The Mishnah places the shofar between two trumpets in the temple at the New Year (Rosh Hashanah 3:3), and the Dead Sea War Scroll (1QM) writes slogans on the trumpets of the end-time army.

common: The silver trumpets are the priests' instruments, and the shofar belongs to the whole people.
uncommon: Some think the 'memorial' blasts of 10:10 were meant to remind God himself to act for Israel, as in a prayer.
